endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Therefore, it is essential to consider additional factors beyond the model’s output when determining eligibility [119].

evidence.title: Integrated Care Coordination for Managing Chronic Conditions: Views of Health Staff on the Implementation of a Program Using an Algorithm to Identify People at Higher Risk of Hospitalisation in Sydney, Australia
evidence.venue: Global advances in integrative medicine and health
evidence.outcome: Staff views on whether the risk algorithm identified all suitable patients for care coordination
evidence.effect: Algorithm identified previously hospitalised patients but missed suitable community patients at increasing risk; clinician referrals were an important additional selection mechanism.
evidence.quote: While the algorithm effectively identified previously hospitalised patients, it did not identify all suitable patients in the community with an increasing risk of requiring acute health care intervention.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring care-management staff to assess patients beyond the AI risk score and refer missed high-risk patients improves program eligibility decisions or outcomes. One qualitative study from Australia found that a risk algorithm missed suitable community patients at increasing risk and that staff saw clinician referrals as an important additional way to select patients.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single supporting study is a level 3 qualitative account of staff views in one Australian deployment. It shows that the hazard exists but does not measure whether added staff assessment changes who enrolls or how patients fare.

Staff reported that the algorithm identified previously hospitalised patients but missed community patients whose risk was rising. This suggests a failure mode in which patients without a prior admission may be excluded before deterioration. Whether a staff review step catches these patients reliably, and how often, has not been measured.

In the one deployment studied, clinician referrals already worked alongside the algorithm as a second selection route, which suggests the practice may fit existing care-coordination workflows. The study did not report staff time, referral volume, or how consistently clinicians applied the referral step.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide rates this practice as a must and states that factors beyond the model output should be considered when determining eligibility. This is a voluntary industry framework rather than a regulatory requirement, and its statement rests on a cited reference rather than on a test of the practice supplied here.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare eligibility decisions made with and without a required staff assessment and referral step, and report how many high-need patients the step adds, the staff time it takes, and downstream outcomes such as admissions and emergency visits for patients the algorithm missed.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether staff review recovers missed high-need patients in these groups, who may be more likely to lack the prior hospital records that the algorithm relied on.
